title: Sachems Who Played in College & Beyond
status: Research in progress; additions require verified college or professional football roster evidence. Saugus, Massachusetts, not Saugus, California.
eligibility: A documented college or professional roster spot qualifies even without game appearances; redshirts, reserves, and practice squads count. Being drafted or invited to a tryout does not alone establish a professional roster spot.

entries.name: John “Jack” Leahy
entries.notes: Earned football letters in 1929, 1930, and 1931. The contributor-supplied newspaper clipping “Saugus Big Boy on DePauw Eleven,” datelined October 20, 1931, identifies him as a 216-pound guard from East Saugus and the heaviest player on the team. The article previewed DePauw’s Old Gold Day homecoming game against Boston University, which the Tigers won 14–9 on October 24.

entries.notes: Notre Dame reserve center on the 1943, 1946 and 1947 national championship teams. Philadelphia drafted Statuto in the 31st round of the 1948 NFL draft. He signed with Buffalo in the AAFC and went on to play 37 regular-season games with 28 starts for Buffalo and the Los Angeles Rams.

entries.name: Doug Waybright
entries.professional: 1948 AAFC draft selection (Buffalo); professional roster not confirmed
entries.notes: Notre Dame’s historical lineups and 1949 Football Review document his Irish career; a draft selection alone is not counted as professional roster membership. Saugus Class of 1944 verified directly by his senior portrait and activities entry in the 1944 Tontoquonian yearbook (page 28), supplied by contributor; this primary source supersedes the conflicting 1945 retrospective. Waybright was a late-season starter at end in 1944, when his end-zone fumble recovery broke a 7–7 tie against Great Lakes. After two years in the infantry, he returned in 1947 and was part of Notre Dame’s 1947 and 1949 national championship teams.

entries.name: Art Spinney
entries.notes: Boston College Class of 1950. Four-year starter at end and captain of the 1949 Eagles. Twice earned All-New England honors for blocking and receiving. His 24 catches in 1948 set a school single-season record at the time. Inducted into the Boston College Varsity Club Athletic Hall of Fame in 1972. Earned All-Pro recognition with Baltimore and won NFL championships in 1958 and 1959. BC's 2025 historical all-time roster independently lists Arthur Spinney for 1946–1949 and marks him as 1949 captain, corroborating his college roster span. Across nine NFL seasons, Spinney played 94 regular-season games and started 87. He was selected for the Pro Bowl in the 1959 and 1960 seasons.

entries.name: John Nicolo
entries.notes: Four-year football and baseball letterwinner at Ithaca College. An All-American running back on Ithaca's 1979 NCAA Division III national championship football team, he also captained the 1980 NCAA Division III national championship baseball team as its shortstop. Named 1980 Division III College World Series Most Valuable Player after setting tournament records with 12 hits and nine runs. Both Ithaca championship teams have been inducted into the college's Athletic Hall of Fame (1979 football in 2014; 1980 baseball in 2019). After college, played one professional minor-league baseball season for the Auburn Americans in 1980 (42 games, 40 hits in 154 at-bats, .260 batting average, 25 runs). Ithaca’s Hall of Fame credits him with 1,817 career rushing yards and 20 touchdowns, both fifth in program history at the time of its account. His 1979 totals included 880 rushing yards, nine rushing touchdowns and 1,109 all-purpose yards.

entries.name: Steve Gannon
entries.professional: Cincinnati Bengals (signed and released in 1980); New York Giants (claimed on waivers and released in 1980)
entries.notes: All-New England defensive end at Holy Cross; 1975 Lynn Item All-Star at Saugus. In 1980 he signed as an NFL free agent with Cincinnati, was released, joined the New York Giants on waivers, and was subsequently released during preseason roster cuts. Contemporary newspaper clippings document both NFL transactions. Holy Cross Hall of Fame inductee (2020). As a senior in 1979, he led Holy Cross with a then-school-record 143 tackles, earned first-team All-ECAC honors and received the Davitt Award as the team’s top defensive lineman.

entries.name: Gary Quinlan
entries.notes: At Holy Cross, Quinlan played 43 games at wide receiver from 1980 through 1983. He averaged 18.9 yards a catch, finishing with 37 receptions for 701 yards and two touchdowns. His role grew over four seasons, from two catches as a freshman to 19 for 275 yards as a senior on the 1983 team that earned the program’s first postseason berth since 1946. He also returned 16 kickoffs for 240 yards and rushed for 58 yards, giving him 999 career all-purpose yards. Each spring, Quinlan traded his football jersey for a spot in the Holy Cross outfield. He played baseball from 1981 through 1984, stole 17 career bases and captained the team as a senior center fielder.

entries.name: Marc Fauci
entries.notes: Boston University defensive standout (1990–1993), initially a strong safety and later a middle linebacker. As a freshman he made 11 tackles, an interception and two pass breakups against Rhode Island, earning Yankee Conference Rookie of the Week. A two-time BU captain, he led the team in tackles as a junior with 90 (also leading the defensive backfield in fumble recoveries) and was selected by his teammates as a tri-captain for the following season. He transitioned to middle linebacker as a senior, helping the 1993 Terriers finish 12–1, win the Yankee Conference and Lambert Cup, and reach the Division I-AA playoffs. His 1993 honors included first-team All-Yankee Conference, second-team All-ECAC and Associated Press third-team Division I-AA All-American. Boston University Athletics Hall of Fame inductee (2010). These details are documented by five original Boston Globe clippings provided by the archive contributor. BU’s Hall of Fame credits him with second-team All-America honors from The Sports Network and National Weekly Football Gazette, and ranks him in the program’s career top five for solo, assisted and total tackles.

entries.name: L.J. McKanas
entries.notes: Northeastern running back (1997 redshirt, 1998–2001). As a senior he ran for 1,756 yards and 14 touchdowns, averaging 159.6 rushing yards per game. He finished with a Northeastern-record 3,692 career rushing yards and earned first-team Hanson All-America and the Harry Agganis/Harold Zimman Award. He ran for 225 yards on 47 carries in Northeastern’s 35–27 win over UConn in 2000 and had 172 yards and three touchdowns in a 34–30 win over James Madison that season. In 2001 he ran for 223 yards and three touchdowns against Saint Mary’s and a career-high 242 yards against UMass. The Boston Sunday Globe followed his pursuit of an NFL opportunity in April 2002. Northeastern inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 2009. The program’s published career rushing table ranks his 3,692 yards first.
